result.question: Code-organization norms for Python and TypeScript projects (2024-2026) — the gap lanes two prior research passes left unevidenced. Sub-lanes: (1) FILE/MODULE SIZE norms: what established style guides and lint tools actually prescribe or default to (ESLint max-lines and max-lines-per-function defaults, Pylint module/function limits, ruff complexity rules C901/PLR, SonarQube/CodeClimate thresholds, Google/Airbnb style guide guidance); any empirical evidence linking file/module size to defect rates or maintainability; practitioner guidance on enforcing size caps on LLM/agent-generated code specifically. (2) FOLDER STRUCTURE: folder-by-feature vs folder-by-type in TypeScript/JavaScript and Python projects — current practitioner consensus, framework guidance (Angular docs, React community, FastAPI/Django project layouts), the colocation principle. (3) BARREL FILES (index.ts re-exports): current guidance — tree-shaking/bundle-size/circular-dependency/test-performance problems, the 'stop using barrel files' trend, when they're still acceptable. (4) llms.txt: adoption state 2026 and whether coding agents/tools actually consume it — is it worth generating for a code repo? (5) pnpm + monorepo workspace defaults for TypeScript 2025-2026 (pnpm workspaces, turborepo adoption, single-package vs monorepo default for a new project) and pytest + pre-commit convention norms for Python (test layout, naming, fixtures organization).
result.summary: Across the five requested lanes the evidence is strong for size norms and folder structure, but thin-to-absent for barrel files, monorepo tooling, and pre-commit. On size: lint tools converge on low-hundreds line caps (ESLint defaults 300/file and 50/function-when-enabled; Pylint's C0302 too-many-lines message), yet ESLint's own rationale disclaims any objective maximum (100–500 is the "usual recommendation" band), the modern Code Climate successor Qlty gates on complexity (15/function, 50/file) rather than raw lines, and peer-reviewed empirical work actually finds smaller modules proportionally MORE defect-prone (power-law β<1) — the only AI-code-specific size caps (Python 150–500 LOC; 50/function + 250/file via ESLint) come from practitioner blogs, not consensus or data. On folder structure the consensus is clear and well-corroborated: the colocation principle (place code near where it is used) and folder-by-feature (the "module" pattern) are the recommended default for any new project expected to grow, over folder-by-type. pytest strongly recommends the src layout with test_*.py / *_test.py discovery naming. llms.txt is genuinely and widely PUBLISHED by 2026 (all three major AI labs plus auto-generating doc platforms), but the spec frames agent CONSUMPTION as intended-not-confirmed and field data is mixed, leaving its worthwhileness for a code repo unresolved. The barrel-files, pnpm/monorepo/turborepo, and pre-commit sub-lanes produced zero surviving claims and remain unevidenced.

findings.claim: Lint tools default to size caps in the low hundreds of lines and treat raw module length as a defect: ESLint's max-lines rule defaults to 300 lines/file, and max-lines-per-function defaults to 50 lines/function (the latter is OFF by default, so 50 applies only when the rule is explicitly enabled). ESLint's own rationale states there is no objective maximum acceptable file size but that common recommendations range 100–500 lines. Pylint ships a dedicated convention message, too-many-lines (C0302), that frames raw module length as a readability defect, governed by the configurable max-module-lines option (real default 1000; the docs' illustrative example sets it to 15).
findings.evidence: All five constituent claims verified verbatim against official primary docs and unanimously (3-0). ESLint: 'max (default 300)' for files, 'max (default 50)' for functions, plus the verbatim rationale 'not an objective maximum... Recommendations usually range from 100 to 500 lines.' Pylint C0302 'Too many lines in module (%s/%s)... reducing its readability' with '[main] max-module-lines = 15' as the doc example. Two precise qualifiers matter: max-lines-per-function is not in any recommended config (off by default), and Pylint's real default is 1000, not the doc's illustrative 15.

findings.claim: The modern Code Climate successor (Qlty) governs maintainability by a COMPLEXITY metric, not a raw line count: it defaults function-complexity to a cap of 15 and whole-file complexity to a cap of 50, and dropped Code Climate classic's raw line-count caps (file-lines 250, method-lines 25). LOC is still tracked as a maintainability metric/rating but is not part of the gating smell set.
findings.evidence: The cited Code Climate docs URL 301-redirects to docs.qlty.sh (its live successor). Qlty's config reference lists function_complexity = 15 ('Maximum function complexity') and file_complexity = 50 ('Maximum allowed complexity for a single file') as the all-languages default; its 8 code smells include 'High file complexity' and 'High function complexity' but NO raw line-count smell. Caveats (non-refuting): 15/50 is the base default with per-language overrides (Rust function_complexity 20), and Qlty still surfaces LOC as a Size Rating metric. Two related over-reaching claims about parameter-count defaults and the exact eight-check list were REFUTED 0-3.

findings.claim: Empirical evidence contradicts the intuition that larger files are riskier per unit size: peer-reviewed work (Koru et al., 2008, externally validated and independently replicated) finds defect proneness follows a power law D=α·s^β with β significantly below 1.0, so SMALLER modules are proportionally more defect-prone and defects accrue slower than size grows.
findings.evidence: Direction is well-supported by a primary peer-reviewed source across 10 KOffice products (all β<1.0), validated on 2 commercial systems (ACE, IBM-DB) and independently replicated (2010 closed-source study; companion IEEE Mozilla/JBoss/Eclipse study). Two load-bearing caveats keep this at medium not high: (1) 'proportionally' means per-unit — larger modules still have MORE total defects (β>0), so this is NOT evidence that large files are safe overall; (2) all data is human-authored C/C++/Java circa 2008–2014 and says nothing about LLM/agent-generated code. The specific β≈0.32–0.42 range in the claim is imprecise and doesn't match the cited paper's own values (~0.4–0.7). The opposing U-curve/sweet-spot model (Hatton via TAOUP) was separately REFUTED 0-3.

findings.claim: Practitioner guidance prescribes concrete size caps specifically for AI/agent-generated code: one article prescribes keeping Python files between 150 and 500 lines of actual code (blank lines and comments explicitly excluded); another prescribes ESLint 'AI guardrails' of max 50 lines/function (forces extraction) and max 250 lines/file (forces modularity), mapping to ESLint's max-lines-per-function and max-lines rules.
findings.evidence: Both are single practitioner Medium blogs; both were 403 bot-blocked on direct fetch, so corroboration is via two matching independent search-snippet passes plus ESLint's own docs confirming the rule mapping is real (max-lines-per-function default 50; max-lines with a custom 250). These are DESCRIPTIVE claims about what each article prescribes, so blog sourcing matches claim strength — but the specific numbers are individual opinion, not consensus or empirical fact. Notably, the article's stated RATIONALE (that 150–500 LOC is AI-working-memory-specific rather than classical maintainability) was REFUTED 0-3, so only the prescribed band survives, not its justification.

findings.claim: The colocation principle — popularized by Kent C. Dodds — is 'place code as close to where it's relevant as possible': keep related files (component, test, styles, data logic) physically close together in a feature folder, organized by what they belong to rather than by file type. It is the definitional basis of folder-by-feature.
findings.evidence: Core proposition verbatim from the canonical primary source (Dodds, who popularized the term): 'Place code as close to where it's relevant as possible' / 'things that change together should be located as close as reasonable.' Independently corroborated by React's own File Structure FAQ, seanmcp, koenvangilst. One nuance keeping honesty: colocation is technically BROADER than the feature-vs-type folder debate (it also covers colocating state, comments, CSS-in-JS, assets) — the 'i.e. organize by feature rather than by type' gloss is the mainstream corollary reading, not a literal equivalence in Dodds's article. Note the related claim that test files specifically should be co-located was REFUTED 0-3, so test placement is contested.

findings.claim: Current practitioner consensus (2024–2026) favors folder-by-feature (the 'module' pattern) over folder-by-type (the 'layer' pattern) for any new project expected to grow. Feature organization colocates all code for a domain so a new feature is added by adding one folder, whereas folder-by-type requires touching controllers/, services/, models/, and utils/ simultaneously to add a feature.
findings.evidence: Primary source (Substack) states verbatim 'If you are starting a new project today with any expectation of it growing, just start with modules' and the one-folder/treasure-hunt framing. Confidence is medium not high because the primary is blog-tier, but the tradeoff is mainstream, well-documented consensus knowledge corroborated by javapractices.com ('Package by feature, not layer'), ProAndroidDev, Spring Boot guides, and multiple 2024–2026 DEV/Medium articles — none contradicting. Minor idealization caveat: a new feature in practice often still touches routing/DI-registration/shared code, so 'add one folder' describes the tendency, not a literal invariant. Framework-specific layout guidance (Angular/FastAPI/Django) was requested but not independently evidenced.

findings.claim: pytest strongly recommends the src layout (especially under its default 'prepend' import mode, though it recommends importlib mode for new projects), and its test-discovery convention collects files matching test_*.py or *_test.py, and within them functions/methods prefixed with 'test' (optionally inside Test-prefixed classes that have no __init__).
findings.evidence: Both claims verified verbatim against pytest's official goodpractices doc and confirmed identical on the GitHub main branch (not stale): 'especially if you use the default import mode prepend, it is strongly suggested to use a src layout' and the discovery rules 'test_*.py or *_test.py files' with 'test prefixed test functions or methods' inside/outside 'Test prefixed test classes.' Note pytest recommends importlib for NEW projects but prepend remains the DEFAULT, so the src-layout recommendation stands. A stronger claim that pytest recommends a SEPARATE top-level tests dir over colocation was REFUTED 0-3 — pytest documents both layouts, so test placement is not prescribed.

findings.claim: llms.txt has real institutional adoption on the PUBLISHING side by 2026 — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini publish llms.txt for their developer docs, and doc platforms (Mintlify, GitBook, Wix, Yoast SEO, AIOSEO) auto-generate them — but its CONSUMPTION is unconfirmed: the spec frames agent use as intended/expected ('Agents are expected to view or search llms.txt') rather than confirmed automatic behavior, and field evidence is mixed. Whether generating one for a code repo is worthwhile is therefore unresolved.
findings.vote: 3-0 publishing [7]; 2-1 on the two consumption claims [8][9]
findings.evidence: Publishing facts are high-confidence (3-0): all three lab URLs verified live, and platform auto-generation independently corroborated (Yoast press release June 2025, Mintlify/GitBook own docs). Independent third-party counts confirm the spec's self-reported 'thousands of sites' (Originality.ai ~36,120 instances by May 2026, 8.8x YoY; Rankability 8.7% of top-1000). But the two consumption-side claims were 2-1 splits: the spec itself only describes intended behavior, and reality is contested — coding agents (Cursor/Claude Code/Copilot) reportedly fetch it in dev-tool contexts (~51.8% reachability) while Ahrefs found 97% of files across 137k domains got ZERO AI requests, and Google/Mueller stated Google does not consume it. The publishing/consumption gap is precisely the open risk for code-repo worthwhileness.

result.caveats: SUB-LANES WITH ZERO SURVIVING EVIDENCE (requested but not answered): (1) Barrel files / index.ts re-exports — no claim survived, so the 'stop using barrel files' trend, tree-shaking/bundle-size/circular-dependency/test-performance problems, and when they remain acceptable are entirely unevidenced here. (2) pnpm + monorepo/turborepo defaults for TypeScript 2025–2026 — no claim survived; single-package-vs-monorepo default, pnpm workspaces, and turborepo adoption were not evidenced. (3) pre-commit conventions and fixture organization for Python — no claim survived; only pytest's src layout and test-discovery naming were evidenced. SOURCE-QUALITY / TIME-SENSITIVITY: The AI-code size-cap band (Finding D) rests on two single-author Medium blogs that were 403 bot-blocked, corroborated only via search snippets — treat 150–500 LOC and 50/250 as practitioner opinion, not consensus or data. The empirical defect study (Finding C) is human-authored C/C++/Java circa 2008–2014 with an imprecise β range and says nothing about LLM/agent code; 'smaller modules proportionally more defect-prone' is per-unit and does NOT mean large files are safe overall. llms.txt consumption facts are 2026-current but volatile and contested (2-1 votes). REFUTED-CLAIM WARNINGS (do not rely on these): the U-shaped/sweet-spot module-size curve and the 200–400 LOC 'defect-minimizing' band (Hatton via TAOUP) were both REFUTED 0-3; that pytest recommends a separate top-level tests dir was REFUTED 0-3; that test files should be co-located with the files they test (Kent Dodds) was REFUTED 0-3 — so test placement (colocated vs mirrored tree) is genuinely contested with no clear norm surviving. Pylint's max-module-lines real default is 1000 (not the doc's illustrative 15) and ESLint's max-lines-per-function is off by default — cite the defaults precisely.
openQuestions: Barrel files (index.ts re-exports): what is the current 2024–2026 guidance on the 'stop using barrel files' trend — the specific tree-shaking, bundle-size, circular-dependency, and test-startup costs, and the conditions under which they remain acceptable? This lane produced zero evidence and needs a dedicated pass.

pnpm + monorepo tooling: for a NEW TypeScript project in 2025–2026, is single-package or a pnpm-workspace/turborepo monorepo the default recommendation, and what is turborepo's actual adoption level? Unevidenced.

Test placement norm: given that both 'tests in a separate top-level tree' and 'tests co-located with source' were refuted as universal recommendations, what is the actual current norm — and does it differ between the TypeScript/React ecosystem (leans colocation) and Python/pytest (documents both)?

Code-repo worthwhileness of llms.txt: beyond docs sites, do coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot) actually fetch and act on an llms.txt placed in a source repository, given the 97%-zero-requests field data? This is the decision-relevant question the publishing-adoption evidence does not settle.

refuted.claim: The default maximum number of function parameters (argument count) is 5, per-language customizable (e.g., raised to 7 for Python).

The full set of default maintainability checks is complexity- and duplication-based (eight checks: similar code, identical code, function parameters, boolean logic, file complexity, function complexity, nested control flow, return statements); the current defaults contain no raw file-length or function-length (lines-of-code) cap — unlike ESLint's max-lines.

pytest officially recommends keeping tests in a separate top-level directory outside application code, paired with a src/ layout (pyproject.toml + src/mypkg/ + tests/), rather than colocating tests with modules.

Empirical data (Hatton) shows defect density as a function of module size is U-shaped and concave-upwards: both very small AND very large modules have more bugs than intermediate-sized ones — meaning decomposition can be taken too far, not just that big files are bad.
The defect-minimizing 'sweet spot' for module size is 200-400 logical lines of code, holding other factors (e.g. programmer skill) equal — a concrete, citable size band for the size-norms sub-lane.

The rationale for the cap is AI-code-editor-specific, not classical maintainability: files in the 150-500 LOC range let AI agents hold the whole file in working memory without truncation and grasp the full scope of a change.
Test files should be co-located with the file(s) they test rather than mirroring the src/ tree in a separate top-level test/ directory.
